speaker: Craig Fuller
title: We're In the Midst of Trucking Bloodbath 2.0
question: In freight logistics, how does the freight brokerage business model hold up during a severe trucking downturn?
guest: Freight brokers have one of the highest returns on capital of any industry, whereas asset-based trucking has the lowest. Because brokers don't actually own anything outside of computers and maybe some real estate, they're not going to just suddenly go bankrupt—they can downsize their operations. A freight broker floor looks like a commodity trading floor, and they depend on two KPIs. One is the spread between spot and contract, which is as wide as 90 cents a mile right now compared to 35 to 50 cents normally. As long as that delta is so high, on a per-transaction basis freight brokers are actually making a lot of money. The problem is there isn't any volume for them. Shippers—big box retailers and manufacturers—want to do business with people who have assets. They want to know who is hauling their load and make sure it's not brokered out to somebody who's going to steal the cargo or lose track of it. So shippers are saying, 'I want to work with asset-based carriers,' and that overflow volume is drying up. The spreads are incredibly high, but the volume of transactions is quite low.

points.core: Asset-light brokers avoid bankruptcy by downsizing headcount during downturns.
points.note: Accept: brokers own virtually no trucks or physical assets, earn high return on capital, and flex operating costs down rather than going bankrupt. Do not credit: claiming brokers are immune to downturns.

points.core: Wide contract-to-spot spreads make each brokered transaction highly profitable.
points.note: Accept: falling spot rates relative to contract rates expand per-load gross margins for brokers. Do not credit: claiming broker per-load margins collapse immediately when spot rates fall.

points.core: Shippers shift volume directly to asset-based carriers for cargo security.
points.note: Accept: when capacity is abundant, shippers prefer asset-owning carriers to verify who hauls freight and avoid theft or lost custody. Do not credit: generic mentions of customer loyalty without referencing asset-based preference or cargo risk.

points.core: Drying overflow freight leaves brokers with high margins on low volume.
points.note: Accept: overflow loads from large carriers dry up, creating a transaction volume crunch despite wide spreads. Do not credit: generic statements that overall economic demand is down without distinguishing spread versus volume.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Freight brokerage is more resilient than asset-based trucking in a downturn, but it is far from immune. Because brokers own no trucks, their costs are largely variable: they have no equipment payments or idle drivers, so they can shrink headcount and stay cash-positive when carriers are bleeding. Early in a downturn they often benefit, since spot rates paid to carriers fall faster than the contract rates charged to shippers, widening the gross margin per load.

That advantage fades as the slump drags on. Shippers rebid contracts lower, volumes shift back to asset carriers offering cheap contract capacity, and revenue per load drops, so even a steady margin percentage yields fewer dollars to cover staff and technology. The 2022–2025 freight recession showed this clearly: C.H. Robinson, RXO and Landstar saw sharp profit declines and layoffs, while heavily leveraged or venture-funded players like Convoy collapsed outright.

The model typically survives, but with compressed earnings, and well-capitalised, efficient, diversified brokers tend to take share from weaker ones. The bigger risk comes at the turn, when spot rates spike while contract prices are locked in, squeezing margins.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
In the early stage of a trucking downturn, freight brokerages hold up surprisingly well. Because the model is asset-light, brokers avoid the heavy fixed costs of idle trucks, equipment debt, maintenance, and driver wages. Gross margin percentages even expand initially, as spot carrier rates plunge immediately while existing shipper contract rates lag behind.

In a prolonged, severe downturn, however, those advantages erode sharply. Once contracts reset lower and capacity turns abundant, shippers shift freight back to direct asset carriers at depressed contract rates, starving brokers of high-margin spot volume. Falling load counts and fierce price competition crush net revenue per load, exposing fixed overhead like excess headcount and heavy technology spending built up during boom years. Working capital strain and double-brokering fraud also intensify, since brokers pay carriers quickly while waiting weeks to collect from shippers. Ultimately, disciplined, scaled incumbents survive better than leveraged carriers by cutting staff and automating, whereas high-burn or undercapitalized brokers frequently fail or consolidate, as seen in Convoy’s 2023 collapse.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Freight brokerage holds up better than asset-based trucking in a downturn, but it is far from immune. Because brokers own no trucks, they avoid the debt, depreciation and idle-equipment costs that bankrupt carriers. Their main cost is people, and they can cut headcount quickly.

Their profits get squeezed, though. Early in a downturn, spot rates fall faster than the contract rates brokers have agreed with shippers, so margins can widen briefly. Then shippers rebid their contracts lower, volumes drop and competition for loads gets fierce, so gross margin per load and total revenue both shrink. The worst stretch often comes when the market starts to recover. Spot rates rise before contract rates reset, and brokers end up paying carriers more than they're getting from shippers.

The 2022–2025 freight recession showed this pattern. Convoy, a venture-backed broker, collapsed in 2023. C.H. Robinson, RXO and Landstar saw revenue and earnings fall, and RXO bought Coyote as the industry consolidated. Survivors relied on cost-cutting, automation and AI to raise output per employee, along with stronger defenses against cargo theft and double-brokering fraud, both of which rose. Scale, technology and a strong balance sheet decide which brokers come through.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Freight brokerages generally weather severe trucking downturns better than asset-based carriers because their asset-light model avoids heavy fixed costs like truck payments, maintenance, and idle driver payroll. Early in a downturn, brokers often benefit from a temporary margin tailwind: spot rates paid to carriers drop faster than contracted rates billed to shippers, expanding gross profit margins.

However, a deep, prolonged downturn still puts significant pressure on the model. As shippers rebid contracts at lower rates and spot freight dries up, both top-line revenue and gross profit dollars per load shrink, even if percentage margins remain steady. Intense competition for scarce loads further compresses spreads. While carrier costs and sales commissions flex down automatically, brokerages still carry fixed overhead in salaried staff, technology, and offices, which squeezes operating income and frequently triggers layoffs or consolidation among undercapitalized or high-burn brokers. On the plus side, falling revenue releases working capital, helping well-managed, scaled brokerages preserve cash and gain market share as weaker rivals exit.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Freight brokerage can weather a severe trucking downturn better than asset-heavy trucking, but a prolonged slump still squeezes profits. Brokers earn the spread between what shippers pay and what carriers charge. Early in a downturn, spot trucking rates can fall faster than contracted shipper rates, temporarily widening that spread. Brokers also avoid the cost of owning and financing trucks that might sit idle.

As the downturn drags on, shipment volumes fall and shippers renegotiate rates. Competition for fewer loads can shrink gross profit per shipment, even when trucks are cheap and easy to book. A broker can therefore report a higher gross margin percentage while earning less gross profit in dollars. Brokers with diversified customers, disciplined pricing, and enough cash to pay carriers while waiting for shippers to pay are better positioned to ride out the slump.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Freight brokers can weather a severe trucking downturn better than carriers that own trucks because they buy transportation as needed and earn the spread between what a shipper pays and what a carrier charges. Early in a downturn, excess capacity can push spot trucking rates down faster than shipper contract rates reset. A broker may earn more per load even as revenue falls.

That cushion can fade as shippers rebid contracts and competing brokers cut prices. If freight volumes also fall, a broker handles fewer loads to cover payroll and other overhead. A higher gross margin percentage can therefore coexist with lower total profit. The asset-light model provides flexibility, but in a prolonged downturn, survival still depends on shipment volume, cost control, and enough cash to pay carriers while waiting for shippers to pay.
